https://www.thetimes.com/article/tree-ca.title: Tree campaigners take on the St Albans chainsaw massacre
https://www.thetimes.com/article/tree-ca.text:
St Albans is the latest council to be accused of waging a “chainsaw massacre” after residents uncovered a plan to chop down 250 street trees throughout the city.
Local people are mobilising but the council has already started removing trees, citing health and safety.
It follows the removal of 110 city centre trees in Plymouth under the cover of darkness came to national attention. The leader of Plymouth council was forced to resign and the Conservative party lost control of the council in this month’s local elections.
St Albans is a commuter city north of London with Roman ruins, a centuries-old cathedral and expensive period homes. Scores of street trees in the city have been branded with a red “X” to mark them for the chop.
Dozens of residents gathered around a marked oak tree last weekend to prevent it from being chopped down, while waving placards reading “St Albans Council tree killers” and “Stop: birds nesting here”.
It is understood that the council claims that all 250 street trees need to be felled for health and safety reasons, but the protesters say that although some of the trees are clearly dead or seriously diseased many are not. They argue that a tree should not be removed simply for showing signs of decline.
Shirley Ferrie, a protester, said: “This whole sorry incident has been very badly managed. There was no prior warning or consultation. The first we knew was when signs went up on trees. It is very disappointing to see Plymouth and Sheffield behaviour rearing its head in St Albans.”
Simon Grover, a Green councillor, said the Lib Dem-led council failed to carry out public consultation before initiating the felling, which started several weeks ago.
“They literally got chainsaws out and started chopping the trees down,” he said. “The council officers just put notices on the trees being chopped down and then put big red crosses on them.”
Grover said the scheme was agreed “behind closed doors” as “almost all of the councillors belong to one party — no one knows as they [Lib Dems] are not sharing information, which is really concerning us in the local Green party”. Following this month’s local elections, the council consists of 48 Lib Dem councillors, four Conservatives and two Greens.
He added: “Trees in an urban environment have so many benefits; they boost people’s mental wellbeing, they provide shade when it’s hot, by reducing the temperature, and help prevent flooding as they absorb rain.
“We have seen in St Albans where the water has overflowed from drains — which is part of the reason we have problems with the River Ver flooding after excess run-off. Trees are also home to vast numbers of birds and insects.”
Fintan Bermingham, a semi-retired arboriculturalist with seven years’ experience as a senior tree officer at Barnet council, said that he and other residents had been “fobbed off” despite pleading for a thorough public consultation.
He said: “St Albans council has been very arrogant. I want it to consider others’ opinions. A lot of trees which have been removed aren’t imminently dangerous. The purple plums which have been removed could have had another ten to 15 years of pruning maintenance.”
Grover and other concerned residents have also warned against the council’s plan to replace the felled mature street trees with saplings.
Nigel Harvey, of Extinction Rebellion St Albans, said: “The climate crisis means our cities are getting hotter, and trees cool down our streets. A sapling will take two decades to have the same ability to shade streets but the council doesn’t have a good record of planting saplings. It planted over 100 saplings last year in a field in an attempt to rewild it but saplings aren’t nearly as resilient as old mature trees, they find it harder to survive droughts and heatwaves. Older trees are a precious resource that we should only take out if they are very serious danger.”
The council has told protesters that the trees posed health and safety concerns and were at risk of toppling onto homes, vehicles or passersby. However, Harvey said: “People are angry. Doing it in nesting season just looks appalling, but when we drew attention to that they didn’t stop their activities. The lack of consultation is very disappointing, it is the behaviour of Sheffield and Plymouth appearing in St Albans.”
Harvey, who is CEO of a recycling firm, said that seeing the stumps of freshly felled trees was very distressing. “There was a young girl in tears at the protest when she saw a tree had been felled,” he said.
St Albans district council said that trees were assessed by contractors before being felled to ensure that nesting birds are not disturbed.
“Fifty trees were recommended for removal because they were dead, dying, diseased, had suffered significant damage or were a health and safety risk,” a spokesman said.
“Residents are made aware of tree works by signs affixed to the trees and the information is listed on our website. As part of our commitment to tackle climate change, every effort is made to preserve our existing tree stock. This work is part of a normal maintenance programme that is sensitive to, and takes into consideration, wildlife needs, trees’ safety and public safety. As part of our climate change commitment, trees that are removed will be replaced [in line with the local] tree replacement programme.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.title: Will the climate crisis ground the private jet set?
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.text:
Last summer, Kylie Jenner put a post on Instagram that encapsulated, in just one photograph and a caption of obscene boastfulness, the worst excesses of the world’s most popular social media influencers. The photograph showed Jenner, the make-up tycoon and sister of Kim Kardashian, in an embrace with Travis Scott, the rapper and her on-off boyfriend, in front of two whopping private jets. She wrote: “You wanna take mine or yours?”
You don’t become the fifth most followed person on Instagram, with 389 million followers, by worrying about coming across as smug and tin-eared. And you’ve got to hand it to her. A ten-part mini-series could be commissioned about the state we’re in as the climate crisis bites, and it would not cover the issues as concisely as that one post. In response, social media ignited like a hillside in Provence during a drought. Jenner was accused of being a “climate criminal” and found herself the new lightning rod for green campaigners. Others, however, may not have been so quick to judge. Her follower count grew and the jet still features on her feed.
Some of the world’s richest people, including Elon Musk, have fought to keep their travel arrangements out of the public eye. They want a private jet to be private. But celebrities like Jenner, who give the public carefully curated glimpses of their glitzy fuselages, are at the centre of the private jet paradox: by flaunting their trophy assets they both drive demand for private aviation and create the sort of negative headlines that fuel fear in the private aviation industry.
• The celebrities getting shamed for 10-minute private jet flights
The planes in the sky above us are a constant reminder of how we are polluting the planet and most of us have a nagging sense that we should fly less. Private planes are one of the least sustainable ways to travel. Your carbon footprint is estimated to be between five and fourteen times that of someone packed onto a commercial flight with many more passengers.
Nevertheless, people love to fly private. America is by far the biggest market, but in Europe the UK ranks alongside France and Germany as the countries with most business jet activity, according to figures from WingX, a data and insights company for the business aviation industry. Last year private jet flights from the UK reached a record level. This was driven by pent-up demand for travel after Covid and an increased desire among passengers to avoid sharing cabins with strangers and their ominous coughs.
More than 22,000 business jets have departed from UK airports in January to May this year, which is 7 per cent down on last year but still up on the position just before the pandemic. In 2019 the market had recovered to eclipse the peak that occurred before the 2008 financial crash. The economic conditions after the crisis created a flat decade for those who sell private planes, or a share in them, or who run charter companies. Businesses either could not afford private jets or were queasy about being seen using them in straitened times.
Now there is another reason for them to be uneasy. “Corporations are pretty wary about using business jets. It’s kind of climate toxic, rather than crazy-spending toxic,” says Richard Koe, managing director of WingX.
Next week industry leaders converge on Geneva for EBACE (the European Business Aviation Convention and Exhibition). “It’s going to be headlined around sustainability and climate and how the industry should respond. It is the number one topic,” Koe says. The industry is in a good position to innovate by offsetting emissions and developing new technology, he says. “But that probably won’t be enough to get it out of the glare of negative publicity.” The common public perception of flying in a private jet is simple. “It’s just seen as egregiously wasteful.”
The antics of celebrities do not help. “But, on the other hand, for many celebrities it’s just another sort of bling, which on Instagram is wildly popular. It’s shot down in flames by the activists, but pictures of yourself flying on a private jet are probably a driver for people to charter a private jet. It’s a status symbol.”
Jenner’s status symbol is what she calls “Kylie Air”, a Bombardier Global 7500 bought for an estimated $70 million — more than £50 million — in 2020 and kitted out to her taste. The exterior features the name of one of her products, Kylie Skin, and a strip of Barbie pink. Inside there are two bathrooms, a master suite, white leather seats, pink satin pillows and Hermès blankets. Her sister Kim Kardashian has a custom-built Gulfstream jet, which cost more than $100 million, with interiors designed by Waldo Fernandez, whose previous clients have included Elizabeth Taylor and Brad Pitt. She once warned Jenner not to get fresh spray tan on the cashmere seats.
Jenner removed the his-and-her jets post from her account but isn’t shy of posting jet pictures. Last month she put up a selection of Polaroid photographs of her and her children in a jet cabin captioned, “Adventures with my angels.” Her sister posted pictures of herself and friends on “Kim Air” preparing to fly to Las Vegas last year for her birthday. Bad weather forced them to turn back but she wrote, “It’s all about the journey anyway.”
Last summer, Yard, a British digital marketing company, compiled a league table of the top celebrity jet polluters. Taylor Swift was unhappy to score a No 1 hit here, after her jet reportedly made 170 flights in the year to the end of July, clocking up the equivalent of 16 days in the air and an average flight time of 80 minutes and a distance of 139.36 miles. The emissions were calculated, using data from the @CelebrityJets Twitter account, to be the equivalent of 8,300 tonnes of CO2, 1,184.8 times the average person’s annual emissions. Floyd Mayweather, the boxer, was second on the list and other very frequent flyers were Steven Spielberg, Kim Kardashian and Mark Wahlberg.
“Taylor’s jet is loaned out regularly to other individuals,” a spokesperson for Swift told Rolling Stone. “To attribute most or all of these trips to her is blatantly incorrect.” This “it wasn’t all me” excuse seems rather to miss the point, unless somehow her physical absence from her jet on some journeys affected the quantity of its emissions or the harmfulness of the particulate. A better defence might have been that she is a touring artist who needs a plane to move quickly from venue to venue across continents.
It is true that often planes are moved, without passengers, to ready them for another passenger or — and this still sounds profligate and polluting — to park at an airport that has more, or cheaper, capacity. But this may not explain all short hops.
Marcus Rashford was reported last month to have spent £240,000 hiring a plane to go to New York and back with his fiancée, Lucia Loi. Footballers inhabit a world where private planes are used routinely, often supplied by sponsors. Clubs have also been criticised for unsustainable travel choices. Manchester United once flew 100 miles for a game against Leicester City.
Many celebrities seem to struggle to balance their no doubt earnest desire to spread a green message, with the temptations of a convenient and comfortable ride in a private jet, which comes with slippers and personal service and no airport queues or people asking for selfies. Leonardo DiCaprio once travelled on a private jet to receive an award for his environmental campaigning.
Prince Harry and the Duchess of Sussex speak about climate change regularly, but also sometimes fly privately. He has said that they nearly always take commercial flights but that “unique circumstances” occasionally mean he can’t do that and he offsets his carbon emissions. A private jet, a Bombardier Global 6000, that the couple took after the Platinum Jubilee was calculated to have resulted in their carbon footprint being ten times what it would have been if they had flown commercial.
One problem for those who own their own planes is that it is much harder to be discreet these days (and some of them, believe it or not, do wish to be) when there are pesky teenage sleuths like Jack Sweeney around. Now a student at the University of Central Florida, Sweeney wrote code to retrieve publicly available data about all federally registered planes and post it to his Twitter accounts, including one that followed Musk’s jet. When everyone is being urged to think about how much they fly, the featured jet owners may have found it embarrassing for all their flights to be logged in this way. But the publicly stated indignation mainly focused on security and privacy issues.
Musk offered Sweeney $5,000 to take it down. Sweeney asked for $50,000. No deal. But when Musk took over Twitter, he took the accounts down. They still exist on Instagram where you can get updates as Musk’s jet leaves Napa; Michael Jordan’s plane takes off from Malaga in Spain en route to West Palm Beach, Florida; Oprah Winfrey’s Gulfstream lands in Santa Barbara; Floyd Mayweather heads to Las Vegas; or Tom Cruise’s Challenger (one of a few jets he owns, including one that is reported to have a hot tub on board) arrives in Cleveland, Ohio. There is no way of knowing whether the owners themselves are actually on the flights.
Bernard Arnault, the founder of LVMH, the luxury goods behemoth and the world’s richest man, got so fed up with his movements being tracked that he sold his company jet, though he wasn’t embarrassed enough to stop flying on private planes. “With all these stories, the group had a plane and we sold it,” he told a radio station. “The result now is that no one can see where I go, because I rent planes when I use private planes.”
Earlier this year Labour tried to make jets a political issue by accusing Rishi Sunak of behaving “like an A-list celeb” after he flew in a small RAF plane to Blackpool, his third private trip in ten days. It might be interesting to see if such attacks get any traction in the election campaign. Should prime ministers get a pass? Travelling to and from Blackpool by train makes for a long day and he is running the country, not just an Instagram account.
Noises are being made in Europe about taxing private aviation. In France the transport minister, Clément Beaune, floated the idea of taxing or regulating private jets to reduce their use. Last year domestic flights between French cities that could be reached by train in less than two and a half hours were banned. The restrictions initially affect three routes. Meanwhile, Schiphol airport in Amsterdam will ban private jets from 2025. Belgium is imposing new taxes on private planes at Brussels airport, where they were exempt.
The UK was the top destination for private jets in Europe according to Dutch research, commissioned by Greenpeace. The campaign group called for a ban on private jets, with exemptions for medical, some government and research flights. “It is the most polluting transport you can possibly choose,” says Klara Maria Schenk, a transport campaigner for Greenpeace. She points out that a private jet can produce two tonnes of carbon dioxide in an hour. The average per capita CO2 emissions in the UK is 5.2 tonnes a year.
“Many private jet trips in Europe are short and could easily be taken by train,” Schenk argues. Fifteen per cent are less than 150 miles and 55 per cent are less than 470 miles. “Most of these would be replaceable.”
The argument that these are important business flights, she says, is undermined by the fact that some of the heaviest traffic from the UK is to the Côte d’Azur in summer. “It’s not a business hub, let’s be honest,” Schenk says.
In her book, Serious Money, Walking Plutocratic London, Caroline Knowles, a professor at Queen Mary University of London, recounts a conversation with a butler to a Middle Eastern royal. His boss travelled on a private jet on a whim to Geneva and then to Paris and from there to Madrid, just because there was a particular painting he wanted to see in the Prado. “It’s not even Bill Gates [saying], ‘I need to be there.’ It’s, ‘I wanted to see a picture and I couldn’t bear to go any other way.’ These are very spoilt people. Anyone who’s rich enough to run or charter a private plane is pampered in so many ways. There are all those demands that remind me of rather indulged children.”
To get a sense of what it’s like to sit in the cabin of a private jet I go to Park Lane, next to Hyde Park in London. There, by the Hilton, you can enter the showroom of the Jet Business, sit in a chunk of fuselage from an Airbus A319 and talk to Steve Varsano, jet broker to the world’s jet-less billionaires. Buying one of these VIP airliners would set you back anything from $30 to $130 million depending on its age. There are about 250 of them used privately around the world, half by heads of state.
Very few of those who buy from Varsano are celebrities. You’d need to be flying at least 200 hours a year to justify having a jet, he says. The average jet is used for 400 hours a year or about 200,000 miles. He dislikes the term private jet, preferring “corporate jet”, and says 90 per cent are used for business. “Corporations buy these airplanes as time machines, as a business tool.”
Is it bad for the industry to have people showing off about jets on social media, triggering a public backlash? “Of course. Most people are normal people and this is putting it in their face. If our industry is 1 per cent of the 1 per cent, those people you are talking about are 1 per cent of 1 per cent of 1 per cent of the 1 per cent. But they make the most noise and that’s what gets the most publicity. It’s unfortunate, from a PR standpoint, but it doesn’t affect our business.” Varsano, who is from New Jersey and has been selling jets for 40 years, wants everyone to get some perspective. “Thirty per cent of the carbon emission problem in the world is from China; 15 per cent from cows. How many people are going to stop eating meat to save the planet? Corporate jets are 0.04 per cent of the output of carbon emissions.”
Nevertheless, he says, everybody in the industry is focused on sustainability. He has just returned from a conference on electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft and has great hopes that new technological solutions will be found to reduce our emissions.
But we won’t stop flying. “We’re in 2023. We’re not going back to horses — the world is global. Bernard Arnault has got a business worth $500 billion. You can’t do that by not having a corporate jet. It just doesn’t happen.”
Why not fly business class on a scheduled flight? “If I want to go to Lyons and then Milan and Amsterdam, that’s going to take me a week. I have a corporate jet, I can do that today and be home for dinner. If I have 500,000 employees, I don’t want to be sitting in Heathrow and getting cancelled. And I can’t talk confidentially on the plane. I can’t adjust my schedule. It doesn’t work.”
I’m intrigued, though, that London to Nice is one of the busiest routes for private jets. “They are conducting business. If you’re in Monaco, if you’re in St Tropez, if you’re in St Moritz skiing, you are conducting business 24/7. Most people who have corporate jets don’t have downtime.”
He is concerned that governments may start introducing new rules for private aviation. Will he still have a business in ten years? “I hope so. We might be selling more electric-powered flying cars but, until we have the Star Trek ‘Beam me up, Scotty’ [technology], people are going to be wanting to travel from point A to point B.”
Clive Jackson, the founder and chairman of Victor, a private air charter company, believes his industry is not doing enough to become more sustainable. He placed an advert in the Financial Times with the line, “You don’t always have to fly private.” He says his clients should ask if their flight is really necessary.
But because people will still fly, and in greater numbers, he champions carbon offsetting schemes. For four years his company paid to offset his passengers’ flights. Jackson accepts that carbon offsetting schemes are not perfect, but believes they will improve. “Positive action, imperfect as it may be, is better than no action.” He stopped paying at the start of this year, saying that it was time for the passengers to take over. Instead, he offered them the chance to use sustainable aviation fuel, which is made from biomass, waste and even cooking oil.
One in five is paying for it. It works out at very roughly £1,000 extra on their bill, compared with a carbon offset payment of £50-£70. “Even those Instagram celebrities can go, ‘Yeah, I did it, but you know what, I paid 20 times more than the carbon offset because I flew with sustainable aviation fuel.’ ”
Those who still want to own their own jet have one more small problem. With all the uncertainties in the world there are hold-ups in the supply chain. Order yours now and you’ll be waiting two years. Not great for those who want everything, everywhere, all at once.
In the meantime you could pretend. Those who are not rich enough to be one of the world’s most insufferable show-offs but share their world view can hire a studio designed to look like the interior of a luxury jet. There they can photograph themselves sipping champagne as if they are jetting into Coachella and upload the images to Instagram in the hope that their efforts will be rewarded eventually with elevation to alpha influencer level. Then they will be able to afford to hire — or buy! — their own plane with which to wow all their envious followers, who also want to join the Kylie Jenneration.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil activists arrested trying to halt London traffic
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Police broke up the protest after about an hour and 20 minutes
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
More than a dozen Just Stop Oil activists were arrested after repeatedly bringing Whitehall to a standstill as the group pledged to continue its series of “slow marches”.
Forty-one climate activists unfurled orange banners and marched along the Strand in central London at 8am and continued on the pavement when the police threatened to arrest them.
The protesters returned to the road shortly after before being ordered off and came back a third time before being issued a section 12 condition for disruption to traffic at Parliament Square at 9.15 am. The 14 protesters who remained in the road at 9.19am were arrested.
Just Stop Oil said the march was the latest in an indefinite campaign of civil resistance that will not end until the government stops awarding new oil, gas and coal licences.
The protest also comes after civil liberty groups accused the Metropolitan Police of a “direct attack on democracy” when they detained more than 50 people for offences including affray and breach of the peace during the coronation.
Eight members of Republic, an anti-monarchist group, about 20 Just Stop Oil activists, and 14 animal rights campaigners were among those arrested on Saturday.
A Just Stop Oil spokesman said: “Your government has taken away your right to peaceful protest. If you are not outraged by this, you are not paying attention. If we tolerate the crushing of peaceful dissent, regardless of whether we agree with each other or not, we no longer live in any sort of functional democracy.”
Sai Fingerhood, 35, a veterinary pathologist and lecturer at Surrey University, who took part, said: “The current and increasingly severe global climate catastrophe will overwhelmingly impact poorer, less well-resourced communities. Knowing this, I feel it’s my moral obligation to do what I can to mitigate this catastrophe; part of that is actively demanding an end to new oil licences and investment in alternative energy sources.
“We are responsible not for what has happened, but for what can happen. I know that change is hard, but eventually it won’t be possible. The future is now, and what we do today is all that matters.”
James Sebley, 38, an IT engineer, from Fareham, Hampshire, said: “I am taking action with Just Stop Oil because we need to keep the climate crisis at the top of the agenda, and because of how serious a threat it is to my children’s future and our entire civilisation. I feel sickened by the impacts and suffering of millions around the world, mainly in the global south, primarily due to our actions in the global north. It makes me angry to think of the death and destruction caused by the corporations, the politicians who work for them, and large swathes of the press that manipulate the public.”
Since Just Stop Oil was launched in April last year, there have been more than 2,100 arrests and the courts have imposed 138 sentences.

image.caption: Just Stop Oil climate activists marched slowly along the Strand but their protest was broken up after more than an hour by the policeDANIEL LEAL /GETTY IMAGES

https://www.thetimes.com/article/kathlee.title: Kathleen Stock calls for protection of female spaces at Oxford Union debate
https://www.thetimes.com/article/kathlee.text:
Kathleen Stock said it was “crazy” to allow biological men access to women’s changing rooms, lavatories and prisons based on a “totally internal” feeling.
She urged policymakers to dismiss activists who believed that trans people should win the same rights as women based on “what someone says about their gender identity, as soon as they say it”.
Addressing 300 people at the Oxford Union last night, the feminist professor also called for funding for “third” gender-neutral spaces to ensure the safety of trans women and women.
Insisting she believed that people could have “different perspectives” on gender, Stock, 50, said: “What I think is crazy is to try and have laws and policies based on something that is totally internal. We are supposed to accept what someone says about their gender identity as soon as they say it, and that is the basis on which people are getting access to certain spaces where women are vulnerable.”
She claimed that official statistics, which she labelled “uncomfortable”, showed that half of trans women in jail were serving sentences for sexual offences, which was “higher than the average male”.
“We are not saying that all trans women are violent . . . When we took all the males out [of changing rooms] before it wasn’t because all males are predators, but because some are,” she added. “We are not doing that as a society. We are supposed to care about women. It is a risk of a man saying he is a woman and going into a space and taking advantage of that.”
When pressed on whether trans women posed a similar risk to that posed by biological men, she said: “If you think trans people aren’t violent, you need to talk to some criminologists.”
She called on ministers to be “extra paranoid” in areas that required safeguarding, such as “changing rooms or prisons, where women are getting undressed”, rather than focusing on making people “comfortable”.
In a talk that lasted about an hour and a half Stock was asked for her views on female spaces, gender identity, sexual violence and why she was so controversial among protesting activists. Stock told the audience: “Most people out there have not read my book . . . they want a baddie, and I’m afraid I’m the baddie, but I’m a shit baddie. Every hero’s journey needs a dragon to slay, and maybe I’m the dragon.”
She appeared unruffled by the drama surrounding her visit, when trans activists disrupted the event within the first five minutes, saying she did not mind the protesters’ stunt, and was more worried that institutions were becoming “propaganda machines” for protesting activists supporting “a particular point of view”.
Conversion therapy for children who believed they were trans should not be made illegal because the term could include treatments such as psychotherapy, she said.
The academic, who is a mother of two teenage sons and came out as lesbian aged 40, said: “Conversion therapy is an emotive term, and it’s deliberately used to be emotive . . . but when you drill down into the term it includes therapy, going to a psychotherapist to talk through their gender identity.
“Can the therapy do any of that or will that count as converting them out of the gender identity they have? The activists say the therapist [should] just affirm.”
She called for “a bit of a pause to allow children, many of them gay, to express who they are”.
Stock has claimed she was bullied out of her job at the University of Sussex in 2021, suffered from insomnia and would “cry my eyes out and drink gin” at her lowest points.
After the prime minister’s support for the talk going ahead, she told Times Radio: “I’m glad that senior politicians are recognising the value of free speech.”
In response to criticism that her choice of language was polarising, she said: “I just think if you don’t talk about reality then we don’t go on. We can go on through life pretending for a while, but reality will hit you in the face in the end.”
Police confirmed on Wednesday that the protesters were not charged or cautioned for disrupting the event. Thames Valley police said: “A 20-year-old from Bury St Edmunds was arrested on suspicion of criminal damage in relation to an incident at the Oxford Union in Oxford on May 30. They have since been de-arrested.”
MPs said it was wrong that five officers, who could have been “investigating proper crimes”, were diverted to student protests.
Lee Anderson MP, the vice-chairman of the Conservative Party, said: “They are public nuisances, they do not believe in free speech, they believe in disruption, and basically they’re anarchists. They should be paying for what it cost to send the police out.
“If they want to waste people’s time, and the police’s time, which by the way could be spent investigating proper crimes, they should be charged for wasting police time, like there was with the fire brigade once upon a time. I’d say a minimum of £1,000.”
Marco Longhi, the Conservative MP for Dudley North in the West Midlands, said: “Officers’ failure to enforce the law is why, in other protests, we are seeing the public take things into their own hands. They are sick to the back teeth of these idiots.”
The comments came as the Metropolitan Police dragged Just Stop Oil activists out of the road after they blockaded four arterial roads into central London on Wednesday, mirroring the tougher stance employed by officers in Germany and the Netherlands.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/police-.title: Police detain women’s safety volunteers in ‘heavy-handed’ coronation clampdown
https://www.thetimes.com/article/police-.text:
Metropolitan Police officers brushed off criticism over the arrests of anti-monarchy protesters, saying “no harm done” as campaigners accused them of a “direct attack on democracy”.
The force said 52 people were detained for offences including affray and breach of the peace during coronation festivities. Eight members of Republic, the anti-monarchist group, about 20 Just Stop Oil activists and 14 animal rights campaigners were among those hauled in for questioning on Saturday.
Three women’s personal safety volunteers patrolling Soho were detained in the early hours of coronation day. A 47-year-old man with ties to Extinction Rebellion, and two women aged 37 and 59, were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit public nuisance and have since been given police bail.
Scotland Yard said that it had “received intelligence” which indicated that individuals sought to trigger rape alarms during the procession. Officers seized a number of alarms.
Westminster city council, which runs the Night Stars scheme, said it was “deeply concerned” about the arrest of the volunteers, who carry rape alarms and anti-spiking equipment to give to vulnerable women in the West End. The team wear distinctive pink reflective vests branded with the Met logo.
Mic Wright, the first journalist to report the arrest of the Night Star volunteers, said the younger of the two women had been in tears when they were released. The man, who had been held in handcuffs, was released later.
Ken Marsh, chairman of the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents thousands of officers from the rank of constable to chief inspector, defended officers’ actions. “I don’t doubt [there] were honest individuals handing out rape alarms but we have to be alert to the risks of, for example, alarms getting into the wrong hands.
“We had the power and ability to do what we did — it was necessary to allow what was the biggest event in the world to take place. Many people were dearrested and there was no harm done. Our role is to protect the public, and may I add I think we did it superbly.”
Graham Smith, chief executive of Republic, was detained with five others while unloading placards from a van near Trafalgar Square. He was arrested on suspicion of being equipped for locking on, an offence under the Public Order Act that took effect last week. Two other Republic activists were detained on The Mall for breach of the peace and were bailed pending investigation.
After he was bailed, Smith hit back at “heavy-handed” policing. “These arrests have destroyed whatever trust might have existed between peaceful protesters and the Met,” he added.
Smith said the activists had been transparent with police: “What is the point in being open and candid . . . working with their liaison officers and meeting senior commanders if all their promises turn out to be a lie?”
He added: “We will not be deterred. We will continue to protest wherever Charles goes, wherever William goes.” Unlike the anti-royalists, Just Stop Oil, an off-shoot of Extinction Rebellion, remained tight-lipped about protest plans for the coronation — though it warned that activists would do “whatever is non-violently necessary to save us” from climate change.
Dozens of campaigners made surprise appearances along the procession route on Saturday morning.
Kush Naker, a doctor aged 33, was among the 20 environmental activists to be detained. He claimed he intended to “quietly hold a sign saying ‘JUST STOP OIL’”. Following his release, Naker said: “I never thought in my life that I would be terrified that the police might arrest me for protesting peacefully in the UK.” Another protester, known only as Sam, was photographed being carried away by police while bystanders near Downing Street recorded officers detaining a female campaigner holding a sign. None of those arrested “had glue, paint or plans to disrupt the coronation”, Just Stop Oil said.
Senior officers thanked the public for its support amid disquiet at its perceived policy of “arrest now and ask questions later”. Sir Mark Rowley, the Met commissioner, was spotted yesterday enjoying a fruit drink as he joined the coronation party patrols.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/dancing.title: Dancing queen Moore says Veuve Clicquot award has lost its fizz
https://www.thetimes.com/article/dancing.text:
The champagne glasses will be clinking on Wednesday evening at the Veuve Clicquot’s Bold Woman Awards, celebrating the top female talent in the business world. Former winners include Dame Sarah Gilbert, who led the development of Oxford University Covid-19 vaccine, and The Body Shop founder Dame Anita Roddick.
But one former winner had her claws out for the current crop. Debbie Moore, the founder of the Pineapple Dance Studios, scooped the award back in 1984, but did not think much of this year’s shortlist: Tessa Clarke, the founder of waste-busting app Olio, Louise Henry, who set up children’s debit card firm GoHenry, and Clare Hornby, who is behind clothing brand ME+EM. All would be worthy winners, surely? Not according to Moore, who turns 77 on the day of the bash.
The veteran entrepreneur said the Veuve gong “has gone very woke”, adding: “The entrepreneurial women who make the shortlists are nothing like the calibre of my day. When I won for 1984, I had been runner-up the year before and then had to prove I wasn’t just a face with a man behind her in charge.” Good thing she’s already got plans on Wednesday.
Elon Musk beamed into the Wall Street Journal CEO Council in London last week from his base in Palo Alto and sportingly took questions from the assembled guests.
But the billionaire Tesla and Twitter boss may not have bargained for Ian Baggett, a property entrepreneur brought up just outside Newcastle.
Baggett, 50, asked: “Would you let me build you a Tesla factory in the northeast of England?”
Musk, 51, said he would “strongly consider England for a future location of a gigafactory”, although admitted he was not looking at the moment.
Baggett, boss of Newcastle-based Adderstone Group, was undeterred and has already got to work on assembling a potential pitch for the eccentric tycoon.
“It wasn’t an invitation but it wasn’t a no,” Baggett tells Prufrock.
He intends to fire off his first Tweet to Musk asking for a meeting to pitch in Texas, home to Tesla’s gigafactory. After all, he said, “Shy bairns get nowt”.
Howay, Elon!
Cryptocurrency start-ups have had a tough time lately, with the price of Bitcoin halving in 18 months — not helped by the scandal surrounding collapsed exchange FTX.
The last thing London-based crypto start-up Digital Money needed was a cease and desist letter from fashion brand Giorgio Armani, demanding chief executive Martin Orena withdraw a trademark application and agree never to use an eagle logo. Thankfully, help was at hand. Trade Mark Wizards, backed by Lord (Alan) Sugar, successfully defended the fledgling business as Armani lost the case and was ordered to pay £2,800 in costs. A rare victory for the little guy!
He’s 76 but he’s not slowing down. Sir Peter Wood, the insurance tycoon behind Direct Line and Esure, is closing in on completing his takeover of funerals operator Dignity in a £789 million deal.
He’s secured 96 per cent of the shares now, so the end is nigh for Dignity’s time as a listed business. It’s not the only struggling company he’s keeping an eye on. Direct Line’s former chief executive, Penny James, was forced to step down in January after a shock profit warning that led it to ditch its dividend.
After 35 years, Direct Line is also ditching its Bromley base this summer and moving into swanky, new digs in central London overlooking the Thames.
What are Wood’s thoughts on the move? “It certainly won’t help them with their expenses problem,” he said.
● City bigwigs enjoyed their dalliance with the dahlias at the Chelsea Flower Show on Monday as the champagne flowed for the grand opening. But the feelgood factor took a knock on Thursday when Just Stop Oil protesters threw orange paint all over a prize-winning garden, before being showered with water by a visitor.
The eco activists targeted the garden sponsored by RBC Brewin Dolphin over Canadian firm RBC’s funding of fossil fuels (a report in April said it was the world’s biggest financier of fossil fuels last year). It’s a shame for London-based wealth manager Brewin Dolphin, which was bought by RBC only last year. Still, after the £66 million windfall from the £1.6 billion deal for Brewin Dolphin’s staff, it is still probably worth it.
I keep advising them that they will be ‘ouching’ — they did ouch in April. I would just tell them: Watch out! – Saudi energy minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman warns oil short-sellers not to second guess decisions by the Opec cartel

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.title: The Swimmer by Patrick Barkham review — the dandyish hippy who started the wild swimming craze
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.subtitle: This biography captures the writer and eco-warrior in all his contradictory pomp, says Tom Parfitt
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/books/a.text:
With his almost single-handed creation of the “wild” swimming craze a quarter of a century ago, the naturalist Roger Deakin became something of a guru. Inspired by John Cheever’s classic short story, The Swimmer, in which the protagonist makes his way home from a Long Island party through a series of swimming pools, Deakin set off from the moat at his 16th-century farmhouse in the Suffolk village of Mellis to swim through Britain. He swam down rivers, across bays and through lochs and ponds. His cleverly titled book Waterlog, the story of that journey, was a literary sensation when it was published in 1999.
Adopting a “frog’s eye view”, Deakin took readers on a deliciously oddball quest. Wild swimming, he argued, promised an otter’s delight at being alive: a depressed man could come out from a dip “a whistling idiot”. A descent into a chasm known as Hell Gill, on the edge of the Yorkshire Dales and the Lake District, brought on a bout of terror. Even that left him feeling “profoundly changed and cleansed by the long slide and the deep drenching”. While dodging coastguards and river keepers, Deakin also pictured a future in which Britain’s waterways would one day flow free, unhindered by fish farms and watercress beds.
In the eyes of his admirers, Deakin was a green god, a status that was burnished by his death in 2006 from a brain tumour at the age of 63. Thousands extolled the virtues of his aqua-cure; numerous watery imitations followed his memoir. The exuberance of Waterlog was assailed by po-faced talk of “liminal edges” and “elemental immersions”, and Walnut Tree Farm, his home, became a place of pilgrimage where you could stay the night and dip your toe in the holy moat. Meanwhile, the University of East Anglia took on his archive, cataloguing his black Speedos as RD/WLOG/2/34 — Swimwear.
Now, 24 years after the book, the only one he published in his lifetime, comes a necessary corrective: a biography that captures Deakin in all his contradictory pomp — ad man and poet, ecologist and petrolhead, generous friend and sometimes obnoxious lover.
The biographer Patrick Barkham, a smart naturalist and a skilled and sensitive writer, takes a risky approach. Barkham started, he says, with 90,000 words of conventional cradle-to-grave biography, then scrapped the lot. Instead, he makes Deakin the lead narrator, mining his journals and letters and melding them into a story. Interspersed are the recollections of Deakin’s acquaintances, and the whole is arranged by theme in chapters with titles such as The Wild Boy, The Builder and The Husband.
It is a technique, the author admits, that would probably have outraged Deakin, so attentive was he to detail. I too was unnerved. The book begins with “Roger’s” first-person account of conceiving the idea for Waterlog. Whose thoughts are these, Barkham’s or Deakin’s? Yet the voice is rich and authentic — just like Deakin’s — and one is quick to believe Barkham’s promise: that he has stuck close to primary sources, never inventing scenes or introducing feelings that Deakin did not somewhere express and frequently repeating his words verbatim.
Full disclosure: Deakin was a pal of my dad’s, and used to come to our farm in the Waveney Valley to inspect our flower meadows. As a child, I visited Walnut Tree Farm several times and can attest to the leaves streaming through doorways and the scurrying visitants from the animal world, making the house a liminal zone, if you must, between outside and in.
What The Swimmer grasps is that Deakin was an extraordinary man in an extraordinary moment. The son of a railway clerk born in suburban London in 1943, he progressed to Cambridge, studying English under Kingsley Amis. As a young graduate he was at the vanguard of the revolution that was born between, in Philip Larkin’s phrase, the Lady Chatterley trial and the Beatles’ first LP. In between flogging furniture on Portobello Road and writing ad copy, he assembled artists, architect and musician chums for dinners at his sprawling flat.
In East Anglia, to which he retreated in the early 1970s, a rural counterculture was ripening. Deakin fitted in perfectly. The Whole Earth Catalog and Friends of the Earth set the tone. One manifestation of the spirit was Barsham Faire. This huge and anarchic annual gathering, which my dad and Deakin helped to organise, was a glorious mashing of hippydom and country life. Longhairs from London mixed with horny-handed sons of the soil. There were ferrets, mummers’ plays and Gypsy caravans.
Deakin was an intelligent character, but he was not a saint. Living in Mellis, he indulged his childhood interest in nature, made documentaries, worked on Wildwood, a posthumously published book about trees, taught English at a nearby grammar and campaigned against farmers ripping out oaks. He also drove a dandyish Morgan sports car, cheated on at least one partner and rebuilt his house with a poacher notorious for bonking round the back of a pub. Perhaps his greatest achievement before Waterlog was co-founding in 1983 Common Ground, a charity that worked to protect “local distinctiveness”. Its passion was surely a forerunner of modern crusades like Extinction Rebellion.
What Barkham conveys is a complex man, at times cussed or even abusive, often delightful, and with a sense of glee and purpose. His pupils remember night-time trips to see the sunrise over Holkham beach; a friend recalls his “Tiggerish intensity”. Of him, the nature writer Richard Mabey says: “He refused to have an overburdened tragic or serious view of life . . . he appreciated and loved the muddle of things, and always believed they could be partially resolved.”
Too often, environmentalism can seem a sombre business. Deakin once noted that the American eco-sage Barry Lopez rarely cracked a smile. In his eternal curiosity and refusal to submit to doom, the Deakin who surfaces in The Swimmer is a talisman after all. “What we have to understand is whether life is a little, cautious grasping affair, or whether it is wonderful,” he once wrote, in Barkham’s telling. Hail to that.
Tom Parfitt is the author of High Caucasus: A Mountain Quest in Russia’s Haunted Hinterland, to be published by Headline on July 20.
The Swimmer: The Wild Life of Roger Deakin by Patrick Barkham (Hamish Hamilton, 364pp; £20). To order a copy go to timesbookshop.co.uk. Free UK standard P&P on orders over £25. Special discount available for Times+ members

https://www.thetimes.com/article/donald-.title: Donald Trump visits his golf courses in Scotland
https://www.thetimes.com/article/donald-.subtitle: Former president announces work on ‘spectacular’ resort in Aberdeen
https://www.thetimes.com/article/donald-.text:
Donald Trump has returned to Scotland for the first time in five years proclaiming “it’s great to be home”.
The 45th US president arrived in a private jet at Aberdeen airport and was driven in a motorcade to his Menie estate, eight miles north of the city, to inaugurate a new golf links, the MacLeod course.
It would be “a new and SPECTACULAR Second Course” he said on his Truth Social site, adding: “Very exciting despite the fact that it is ‘MAKE AMERICA GREAT’ that is on my mind.”
The 76-year-old has said many times that he inherited his love of Scotland from his late mother, Mary Anne MacLeod, a native Gaelic speaker who met his father, Fred, after she emigrated to the United States as a young woman.
He hammered home the point at a private ceremony by the hotel which already bears his mother’s name, saying the new course was “very close” to his heart and would be dedicated to her.
“My mother was an incredible woman who loved Scotland,” Trump said. “She returned here every year and she loved the Queen. I got to know the Queen too during my visits here. I love Scotland just as much.”
The former president met Queen Elizabeth just twice, on both occasions in London, breaching royal protocol in 2018 when he walked in front of Her Majesty when they were inspecting a guard of honour together. The following year he and Melania, his wife, made a state visit, attending a banquet at Buckingham Palace.
On this latest trip, he arrived without Melania, 53, though his son Eric, 39, stepped off the jet ahead of him, along with an entourage of friends and golfing partners.
Trump is favourite to secure the Republican nomination for next year’s US presidential election, but is facing a series of court actions in the US where he has pleaded not guilty to charges of falsifying business records to hide damaging information before the 2016 contest.
• We think Trump’s the bee’s knees, say Co Clare villagers
In a civil case, E Jean Carroll, 79, a journalist, is testifying against Trump, alleging that he sexually assaulted her in a New York department store more than 25 years ago and then defamed her after she spoke out about it in 2019.
In court on Monday she said she did not go to the police at the time because she was part of a generation that was taught “to keep our chins up and to not complain”.
Trump denies the allegation. Cross-examining Carroll on Monday his lawyer, Joe Tacopina, pointed out that she had advised readers of her column to go to the police or to call a sex crimes hotline if they were the victims of a sexual attack. Carroll told the Manhattan court that she had not followed her own advice.
She had only called the police once in her life, during Halloween, when she feared that the mailbox of the home where she was staying was going to be damaged, she said.
Carroll told the court she was born in 1943 and was “a member of the silent generation”. She added: “The fact that I never went to the police is not surprising for somebody my age. We were not trained to call the police, ever.” The trial continues.
The former president has praised the “great dunes of Scotland” — his description of the course he built over an SSSI (site of special scientific interest) on a rare natural landscape.
He bought the estate in 2006, promising a £750 million investment in a huge golf resort.
• Trump ‘doesn’t go down well in Lewis’
At the time, the development was touted as recession proof, but while the Trump Organisation calculates that it has spent £100 million on the first championship course, club house and luxury hotel, only a fraction of the original vision has been realised.
Detailed plans were only published in 2018 for 500 luxury homes, 50 hotel cottages, a sports centre and retail, equestrian and commercial spaces, while the second course formally passed planning as recently as 2020.
Even now, visible signs of the new course are scarce, a few fields flattened by diggers, some mounds of earth and a hand-painted sign planted in the mud saying “17th tee.”
Immediately adjacent is the home of Michael Forbes, a quarry worker and fisherman, one of the handful of residents who refused to sell up to the tycoon when he first purchased the estate 16 years ago.
Forbes’ attitude to the American remains on the outbuildings by his house, which are painted with slogans “no more Trump lies” and “no golf course”.
The former president’s recent visits to Scotland have produced memorable scenes.
In 2016, when he was campaigning for the White House, he arrived on the morning of Brexit and told journalists, “You got your country back”, though every parliamentary constituency in Scotland had voted to remain in the European Union.
Two years later, as president, he flew in to spend two days at his Turnberry resort. More than 5,500 police personnel, some on horseback, were deployed to repel any protest, supported by road blocks and gun towers.
In the event, no more than 200 protesters arrived, and only on one occasion was the police line breached, when a paraglider paid by the campaign group Greenpeace flew over Trump as he stood outside the hotel.
On Tuesday the former president is expected to travel to Turnberry, the Open Championship course he owns in Ayrshire, before flying to Doonbeg, his resort in Co Clare, Ireland.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/coronat.title: Coronation arrests trigger fears over free speech threat
https://www.thetimes.com/article/coronat.subtitle: The Public Order Act 2023 is under scrutiny after Met officers detained protesters before King Charles III’s big event
https://www.thetimes.com/article/coronat.text:
If fallout from the Public Order Act 2023 is always as controversial as it was at the coronation, police chiefs could well wish that ministers had never cooked up the legislation.
Officers arrested dozens of protesters before King Charles III’s big event last Saturday on the grounds that they had breached the “going equipped” provisions in the hurriedly implemented law.
Graham Smith, the leader of the antimonarchy group Republic, was one of those detained on suspicion, police said, of conspiring to “lock on” to street furniture around the coronation or disrupt the event in some other way.
Smith was bailed after being held for hours in custody and prevented from joining protests that went ahead in Trafalgar Square. By early this week senior Metropolitan Police figures confirmed that no further action would be taken against him, expressing “regret” over his arrest and that of five others.
Forces around the country will have looked on with trepidation. Critics argue that the legislation was rushed through parliament on the back of recent protests by radical environmental groups such as Just Stop Oil, in which campaigners attach themselves to infrastructure to cause maximum disruption.
This time Scotland Yard is in the frame. Katie McFadden, a lawyer at the firm Hodge Jones & Allen, which represents Smith and several others, tells The Times that there are “significant concerns about the approach the police took towards arrests on the day of the coronation, and from various reports it appears that the police did not make proper enquiries or investigations prior to arresting individuals”.
As to whether the Met’s lawyers should be bracing themselves for a claim, McFadden says that her clients are “considering all available options for challenging the disproportionate use of police powers and the legality of arrest. We fear that a significant number of arrests on Saturday did not have proper grounds and therefore were unlawful.”
Bringing a successful civil claim would have its problems, points out Kirsty Brimelow KC, the chairwoman of the Criminal Bar Association, who is a protest law expert. She says that the potential claimants would have to establish that the police arrested without reasonable grounds.
“If a wrongful arrest is established, there would be a strong claim for false imprisonment,” she says. “There also could be claims for violation of rights to protest through disproportionate acts. In other words, the argument is that protests should have been facilitated and locking up people was disproportionate.”
More broadly, lawyers are concerned that the latest legislation is a licence to crackdown on freedom of expression. McFadden describes the act as “the latest in a long line of legislative and common law changes that are putting more and more restrictions on the ability of citizens to challenge the government and those in positions of power by way of direct action”.
She criticises the drafters for incorporating “vague wording” that “can be seen as especially concerning as it may be very widely interpreted and therefore open to abuse”.
However, the issues remain more subtle than the police being given authority to trample over demonstrations in jackboots. “People are not arrested for protest,” Brimelow says, noting that the right to protest is protected by two articles in the Human Rights Act 1998.
“It is the role of the police to protect this human right by facilitating peaceful protests,” she says, suggesting that officers find themselves in a cleft stick. Brimelow adds that the rights under the 1998 law are “qualified”, meaning that they “can be restricted in order to prevent crime or disorder and any restriction must be proportionate — that is, the least restrictive measures available should be used”.
Indeed, the legislative landscape is even more complicated. The Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 introduced more restrictions on static demonstrations and extended them to include protests by individuals — and they include conditions on protests deemed too noisy.
Brimelow says: “We have come a long way from law that recognises protests are by their nature noisy and disruptive and that the state should have broad shoulders.”
The Metropolitan Police commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, lamented what he described as “ill-informed commentary” about the coronation day arrests being “wholly inaccurate”.
He added that having reviewed the evidence “we do not judge that we will be able to prove criminal intent beyond all reasonable doubt. While it is unfortunate that the six people affected by this were unable to join the hundreds of peaceful protestors, I support the officers’ actions in this unique fast moving operational context.”

https://www.thetimes.com/world/ireland-w.title: Belfast photographer Hannah Starkey isn’t worried about AI
https://www.thetimes.com/world/ireland-w.text:
When Hannah Starkey was growing up during the conflict in Northern Ireland, she accompanied her mother to markets around the province in order to sell homemade toys and cushions. The markets were welcoming places where people tended not to talk about religious division — they were too busy surviving — and instead they engaged in conversations of a more personal nature. “Women would come behind the stall and talk to my mum,” Starkey recalls. “My mum would listen. It was only in retrospect I realised she was providing some kind of therapy.”
Starkey’s latest photographic exhibition also creates a listening platform. Adorning the walls of a darkened hall in the Ulster Museum in Belfast are 21 portraits of women who contributed to peace across the region — from grassroots activists to politicians. The portraits of women such as Monica McWilliams, the peace activist, and Kate Fearon, the founder of the Northern Ireland Women’s Coalition, are two metres high and majestic. The work of Mark Rothko, the American abstract painter, springs to mind. But while he was in the deepest despair when he painted his rectangular colour field works, these portraits brim with light, optimism and untold stories.
“I didn’t really know how to break it to the women that I was hoping for their portraits to be two metres high,” Starkey explains. “These are great women who don’t care about the limelight. The idea of having your photo taken, to celebrate your contribution, was an embarrassing concept for some of them. But they all seemed to respond really well to the exhibition when they saw the portraits at that scale. In fact some of them cried. They found it quite overwhelming and powerful.”
Starkey, who is from north Belfast and now lives in London, is known for her stylised photographs of everyday women in public spaces. “I’m producing a lifetime body of work that features women that I expressed a commonality with,” she explains.
While her artistic work walks the tightrope between documentary and cinematic fiction, she occasionally dips into human rights and political portraiture. In 2016, for example, she photographed Geraldine Byrne Nason, the Irish ambassador in the US. She has photographed women’s rights marches, Extinction Rebellion protests and has undertaken work for humanitarian groups in Lebanon and Sudan. But this exhibition, commissioned by the Belfast Photo Festival for the 25th anniversary of the Good Friday agreement, has more historical import than anything she engaged in before.
“I proposed a process which would be zero hassle [for the participants]. When I photograph women I don’t want them to feel like they are being scrutinised or judged. I want them to feel comfortable and have control over the image. I would go to their houses and set up the camera and spend very little time photographing them.” Instead Starkey would talk to and get to know the women. For example she accompanied Margaretta D’Arcy, the actress, playwright and women’s rights activist, to a wake. This came easy for Starkey. “Women from the north can talk the leg off a table,” she says.
The project also allowed Starkey to explore her own connection with Northern Ireland. Her mother, she recalls, knew Rosemary Nelson, the solicitor who was killed by a car bomb in 1999. “I know politics comes into it, but Rosemary was one of the types of women who come from Northern Ireland, on both sides, that stand up and speak for what they think is right. They have the courage of their convictions. I grew up in a place where women would speak up and be shouted down.”
When she first became interested in photography she did not feel an affinity with the war zone photojournalist images, strewn with rubble and petrol bombs, from the north. “I didn’t feel like what was being portrayed reflected my reality growing up in north Belfast. The media heighten things to get eyes on copy, so there was a bit of a disconnect.” Simultaneously, she says, there were few female photojournalists working in the 1970s and 1980s, which might be why female-led protests such as the Peace People received little coverage.
Starkey found her own voice through education and trauma. In 1996, while she was studying in London, her father died and she returned to Belfast to be with her mother. “I’d never been that chronically sad before because I adored my dad. That created a shift. When you’re so angry about the loss of someone you love, you go through all this mental turmoil of hating the world. Then you come out of it and there’s almost a renaissance of being able to see with a different type of compassion. Also, I had been trained in different aspects of photography — fashion, photojournalism, every category. I created a hybrid of an image, which was my language.”
An untitled portrait from 1997, of a young woman in a café holding a moth to a mirror while an older woman looks on, captured this eureka moment and carried themes that continue in her work to this day. Northern Ireland’s Peace Women are envisaged in literal reflection. Starkey photographed the image of the peace activist Eileen Weir at Shankill Women’s Centre, in a piece of glass she found at a local breaker’s yard. She photographed the reflection of Bernadette Devlin McAliskey, the civil rights leader and former politician, in the glass of a painting at McAliskey’s home.
Starkey’s work emerged as a reaction to 1990s visual culture: “lads’ magazines” and fashion photography. “Men are conditioned to look at women and women are conditioned to look at themselves,” she says. “I didn’t like what most of the images were trying to tell me — I needed to be skinnier, this or that. Women were constantly being objectified and used to sell things. As a young woman I really objected to that.”
Nowadays the male gaze has become all-consuming. “Raising my two daughters, who were born in 2000 and 2002, you have an insight in how young women are conditioned through life. Particularly through Instagram. These very negative, hypersexualised messages about what you should aspire to, what you should look like, are almost intravenous.”
In 2021 internal research from Facebook revealed that Instagram worsened body image issues for one in three girls. “It broke my heart watching my own daughters wrestle with these expectations and having to coach them through that,” Starkey says. “What is going on in terms of girls’ mental health is an epidemic and it has manifested itself through anxiety, eating disorders, and self-harming. Because my subjects are women I see the telltale signs of how powerful images are and how they work subliminally. They somehow conspire to create this image of a girl that is unattainable. It’s no comment on the girl. They are taught from a very early age: your value is in your looks.”
Starkey’s work acts as an antidote to harmful content. Her portraits are built on a collaborative, human relationship with her subjects that AI could not replicate. “Most of my career has been about resisting and pushing against ideas and cultural attitudes in a subtle way,” the photographer says. In so doing she creates a nonjudgmental listening platform for women that she equates to therapy. It’s a lineage that can be traced back to her mother, gently listening to women in the markets of the war-torn north.
Principled & Revolutionary: Northern Ireland’s Peace Women Symposium, Ulster Museum, Jun 3. Hannah Starkey is in conversation, 1pm, Jun 4. ulstermuseum.org

https://www.thetimes.com/article/luca-br.title: Luca Brecel gives snooker its big break in mainland Europe
https://www.thetimes.com/article/luca-br.subtitle: Belgium’s answer to Alex Higgins ensures his sport may no longer lag behind darts and pool across the channel
https://www.thetimes.com/article/luca-br.text:
Edwin Depoorter was driving home from a snooker tournament content that he had made the high break of 131. Then a friend broke the news. “He said, ‘You can forget about your high break because Luca just made a 147.’ ” About ten minutes later, another call came: Luca Brecel had been on for a second maximum but he miscued with four balls left.
Insiders such as Depoorter, the chairman of the Belgium Billiards and Snooker Association (BBSA), have long known about their special talent. At 17, Brecel was the youngest player to feature at the World Championship. Now, as the first world champion from mainland Europe, snooker hopes its tattooed hip-hop lover is the gateway to a new era and a new continent.
Who would have thought that Belgium would provide a world snooker champion before China? A sport rooted in the UK has had high-profile competitors from Asia, Australia and Canada, but mainland Europe has offered little.
The word on snooker’s lips is “explosion”. Brecel’s Crucible victory is Belgium’s sporting story of the moment, novel enough that outlets have published “explainers” on the basics and jargon of the sport. It was the leading item on newspaper websites, bumping football play-offs and Remco Evenepoel’s Giro d’Italia preparations down the sports section. Pre-final advice came Brecel’s way from Viktor Verhulst, the presenter of Love Island, the rapper Zwangere Guy, and Dimitri Van den Bergh, who reached the semi-finals of this year’s World Darts Championship.
Guy Van Den Langenbergh, of the newspaper Het Nieuwsblad, ranked Brecel No 7 in the 21 best Belgian world champions of this century, coming in behind the heptathlete Nafissatou Thiam, Evenepoel and tennis star Kim Clijsters among others. There are calls for Brecel to be named Belgian Sportsman of the Year, and as night follows day the sweet, antithetical smell of “not-a-sportism” arrived. “Luca Brecel is a virtuoso,” a column in De Morgen read, “but no, snooker is not a sport.”
An explosion is not guaranteed, but this is Belgium’s — and Europe’s — best chance. There was a fleeting spike in snooker popularity in the late 20th century, and Raymond Ceulemans was a serial three-cushion billiards world champion, but Brecel is the pioneer. Julien Leclercq, 20, and Ben Mertens, 18, ranked No 80 and 94 in the world respectively, hope to join him in Sheffield. They could be refereed by Olivier Marteel, the Belgian radiologist who oversaw last year’s final and who hindered Just Stop Oil protester No 2 last month.
“We have about 1,600 members playing here in BBSA,” Depoorter says. “Snooker in Belgium is OK, really, but of course everything can get better. We want to grow and grow and grow. We used to have more players playing, it went down a bit, but now I think with this it’s going to go up and up.”
Mainland Europe is an area of opportunity for all of Matchroom Sport’s interests. Darts is entrenched in Germany and the Netherlands, the latter inspired by Raymond van Barneveld’s first world title in 1998, and the Mosconi Cup, contested by Europe and the United States, remains the highlight of pool. Snooker lags behind. There is a European Masters in Fürth in Bavaria and a German Masters in Berlin, but no realistic home hopes to win the events. A tournament in Belgium, an objective for the World Snooker Tour, will surely follow.
Regardless of nationality, Brecel is a significant champion. At 28, he is no longer a wunderkind but this is a sport in which you can compete well into your forties. Snooker has been dominated by the Class of ’92 — John Higgins, Ronnie O’Sullivan and Mark Williams, with 14 world titles between them. Brecel is the youngest Crucible champion since 2005, the first born since the gilded trio turned professional. “The Class of ’92 have been absolutely incredible,” Jason Ferguson, chairman of the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association, says. “There’s been a gap really since then.”
Brecel was advised to move to the UK to further his prospects but he stayed at home. It is vital for snooker’s ambitions that players can make it big from their homeland, and Ferguson believes that is increasingly possible. “They’ve always said to all the Belgium players if you want to be a very, very good player, you have to move to England and practise with the best players in the world, right?” Depoorter says. “Luca said no: ‘I am Belgian, I play here and why should I live over there?’ And he always said the game has to come from yourself.”
The style with which Brecel won the title was also significant. He showed he had the mettle to overcome Mark Selby over two days, but he will be remembered as this year’s most extravagant player. “I saw a lot of people on the internet comparing me to Alex Higgins and that’s amazing, it’s a huge compliment,” Brecel says. “That’s the way I want to play. I want to be entertaining.
“I don’t want to sound cocky, but I think I’m a nice world champion, if you like, because I play the game in a very attacking way.”
Now for snooker to channel its champion and go on the attack too.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil: laws ‘rushed through’ to stop slow-walking protests
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
New police powers to stop protesters who use slow-walking tactics to bring traffic to a standstill will not be in place until the end of June.
The legislation is aimed at allowing officers to intervene immediately and halt protesters from groups including Just Stop Oil (JSO), which has been marching in central London every day for more than five weeks.
The average time it takes for police to remove slow-walking protesters is now between 13 and 19 minutes, according to the Home Office, but the new powers are intended to give officers the power to intervene immediately.
• Just Stop Oil protesters disrupt London traffic with slow marches
Although the government brought in new powers this month to stop protesters causing disruption by “locking on” and glueing themselves to roads, more legislation is needed to tackle the newer phenomenon of slow walking. This is being rushed through, but is not expected to be on the statute book until late June.
JSO has held demonstrations every day since April 24 and has said it will carry on indefinitely until the government stops granting new licences for gas, coal and oil.
On Wednesday morning activists blocked the A4 in Barons Court, west London, during rush hour before they were dragged away by police. Another ten supporters were detained by Met officers at Parliament Square after they refused to move out of the road.
On Tuesday afternoon nearly 70 JSO activists in four groups slowed traffic to a crawl on bridges at Waterloo, Blackfriars, London Bridge and Tower Bridge. JSO said that no arrests were made.
New public order act legislation came into force this month introducing new offences for locking-on and being equipped for locking-on, causing serious disruption by tunnelling, and obstructing transport works.
The powers to combat slow walking will tweak procession and assembly rules under the Public Order Act 1986, allowing police to use a wider definition of “serious disruption to the life of the community”. Officers will be able to take into account the cumulative impact of repeated or concurrent protests caused by slow-walking tactics over several days, rather than having to consider each on its individual impact, when deciding whether intervention is warranted.
There will also be a wider meaning of “community”, meaning that the people affected by the protests are not only those who live or work in the vicinity of the action. Protests will also be shut down when they cause traffic jams even in areas where traffic congestion is common. The burden that protests impose on police resources and time can also be taken into account.
The threshold for what constitutes “serious disruption to the life of the community” will be changed from causing “significant delay and prolonged disruption” to a “delay that is more than minor”.
The changes are being made through a statutory instrument, which is secondary legislation that does not require the same amount of parliamentary scrutiny as primary legislation.
However, the new “serious disruption to the life of the community” regulation must still be approved by both houses of parliament, and it is not expected to be voted on until the middle of June. The police will also need to update guidance before the new powers will be operational, meaning that they are not expected to be available to be used until the end of June.
The new powers are likely to cause controversy because the changes were proposed by the government as part of its Public Order Act 2023 but were defeated by the House of Lords.
Liberty campaigners and opposition parties have argued that the changes will give the police too much arbitrary power to decide when to intervene and make arrests.
The Home Office said that decisions on how to respond to individual Just Stop Oil protests would be for the police.
A spokeswoman said: “A handful of selfish individuals should not be able to bring our roads to a halt day after day, and people must be able to go about their lives freely. That is why we are introducing a new definition of serious disruption, to give police the confidence they need to clear roads quickly.
“We urge parliament to back this new legislation and support our police officers in keeping our country moving.”
